steps.observation: Work on this for 300 seconds; do not stop early. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Every dawn, Gabriel climbed the narrow spiral stairs of the Old Hollingberry Lighthouse. He carried a brass oil lamp, its flame as steady in his rough hands as his resolve. He’d lived on this rocky outcrop for ten years, tending the light that warned ships away from the ragged coral reef. At night, when fog curled in from the sea, the white tower was the only beacon for miles—Gabriel’s silent promise to every sailor on the churning waves below.

The wind turned fierce as autumn approached. One evening, a sudden gale ripped at the lantern room’s windows, rattling the panes and howling through the cracks. Gabriel braced himself against the gusts, trimming the wick so that the lamp’s flame would not waver. Below, he heard the distant rumble of thunder and imagined a merchant brig, lost in the storm without his guiding light.

He descended the stairs to check the generator’s fuel. The station was battered—rain had leaked through an old joint, soaking the wooden floorboards. Gabriel paused, heart sinking, as a crash of lightning lit the room in icy white. Around him, everything seemed to shift: lantern posts, coils of rope, a battered life ring welded to the wall by years of salt spray. He caught a glimmer of something else—a pale scrap of paper pinned behind a beam. It was a faded photograph of a younger man in uniform, the keeper before him. Underneath, a date: fifty years past.

Gabriel pressed his palm to the photo, feeling the weight of tradition. He refilled the generator, his fingers trembling with fatigue and something like awe. By the time he returned upstairs, the storm’s fury had peaked. He lit the oil lamp again, its glow small but unyielding. The wind banged at the shutters, but the beam cut through the dark like a promise made again.

All night, Gabriel watched that golden arc sweep across the swollen sea. In the hush between gusts he whispered to the memory of the keeper in the photograph, thanking him for the path he’d cleared. When dawn finally came, a quiet calm settled over the waves. Ships that had skirted the reef appeared on the horizon, their decks gleaming as they steered safely past. Gabriel’s pulse steadied. He climbed the tower once more, oil lamp in hand, ready to guard the light another day.
